Treat prompt injection as an ongoing threat; a prompt disclaimer alone is not a control. Evaluation and memory Use a held-out dataset for groundedness, task accuracy, injection resistance, privacy leakage, tool misuse, latency and cost. Store only necessary user-approved memory with retention and deletion controls. Avoid raw secrets and sensitive identifiers in prompts, embeddings and traces. Detailed Mechanics and Topic Features API design Use explicit request/response schemas, server-side validation, pagination, bounded payload sizes and consistent errors. Authenticate callers and authorize each resource. Add request IDs and per-principal rate limits. Use idempotency keys for retryable mutations and persist the outcome atomically with the operation. Never trust client-reported payment or identity-verification success. Webhooks Verify the provider signature against the raw payload using its documented algorithm and freshness checks. Reject unauthenticated events, deduplicate event IDs, persist receipt and acknowledge promptly before asynchronous processing. Support out-of-order delivery and retries with a state machine. Keep replay tooling and a dead-letter queue. A public endpoint and a secret URL alone are insufficient verification. External calls and files Set timeouts, bounded retries, circuit breakers and cancellation. Apply SSRF controls to user-provided URLs. Validate upload size, content and ownership; scan where appropriate and use short-lived download grants. Store attachments in object storage with tenant-aware access. Treat all third-party content as untrusted data. Contract checks Exercise malformed payloads, missing fields, oversized input, bad signatures, duplicated events, timeout-after-success, dependency outage and rate-limit responses. Document versioning, deprecation and incident ownership. 6. Implementation Pattern and Copyable Code This focused TypeScript implementation belongs in the trusted application or test layer. Process, Inputs and Outputs Step Action Evidence 1 Validate authentication transaction and callback Approved input scope, source and owner 2 Resolve verified identity to active membership Recorded decision, revision and exception handling 3 Create a session at the required assurance level Observed outcome and recovery or rollback decision Stop at any boundary whose required evidence cannot be established. If an external side effect may already have occurred, reconcile its durable identity before retrying. 4. Related Apps, Software and Third Parties Component Role Integration responsibility Duo Approved administrator federation Verify supported contract, least privilege, account access, data handling, quotas and ownership. WebAuthn Passkey authentication Verify supported contract, least privilege, account access, data handling, quotas and ownership. OIDC provider Federated identity Verify supported contract, least privilege, account access, data handling, quotas and ownership. These products are candidates for this capability, not a claim that they are connected to this documentation site. Choose them by boundary responsibility and measured requirements. Keep their private credentials outside public HTML. 5. Detailed Mechanics and Topic Features Methods and tradeoffs Passwords require secure password hashing, recovery and abuse controls. Email OTP proves current access to a mailbox and is not phishing-resistant. Magic links are bearer credentials that can leak through forwarded messages. TOTP uses authenticator-generated time codes; recovery codes need protected storage and one-time consumption. Passkeys use WebAuthn and origin binding. OIDC provides federated sign-in; OAuth alone is delegated authorization. SAML supports enterprise federation. Role-specific policy Create an explicit policy matrix for administrator, user, employee, client, applicant and demo roles. For the user’s projects that specify Duo-only administration, enforce the Duo SSO flow server-side and do not expose an alternative route that bypasses it. Other projects may have different approved policies; do not copy a single app’s policy globally. Employee application SSO and administrator Cloudflare Access protections are separate architectural decisions. Federated sign-in checklist Use supported identity-provider libraries. Validate issuer, audience, signature, expiry, state and nonce where applicable; use PKCE for authorization-code flows. Allowlist redirect URIs. Link accounts only after proving control of the identities; matching an unverified email is insufficient. Apply application roles after identity verification and fail closed if provider checks fail. Enrollment and recovery Require reauthentication for factor changes, email changes and account linking. Notify users of security changes. Protect recovery paths as strongly as sign-in and audit privileged recovery. Plan lost-device recovery, provider outage behavior, account suspension and session revocation. Test denied users, stale roles, invalid callbacks and blocked direct API requests. 6. Implementation Pattern and Copyable Code This focused TypeScript implementation belongs in the trusted application or test layer. Supply identity, permission and provider-verification state from real verified dependencies; do not accept trust flags directly from a browser. typescript interface VerifiedIdentity { issuer: string; subject: string; emailVerified: boolean; } interface Membership { userId: string; tenantId: string; active: boolean; } export function resolvePrincipal( identity: VerifiedIdentity, membership: Membership, approvedIssuers: ReadonlySet<string> ) { if (!approvedIssuers.has(identity.issuer) || !identity.subject) { throw new Error("Unapproved identity"); } if (!membership.active) throw new Error("Inactive membership"); return { userId: membership.userId, tenantId: membership.tenantId }; } // Invoke only after the provider library verifies signatures, // audience, expiry and authentication-transaction protections. Version the implementation with the consuming application and run this chapter’s acceptance checks when its assumptions change. A copied unit does not establish that all external integrations are active. 7. Mermaid Architecture and Process Diagram Authentication & SSO — decision process flowchart TD A["Validate authentication transaction and callback"] --> B["Resolve verified identity to active membership"] B --> C{"Acceptance and policy pass"} C -->|Yes| D["Create a session at the required assurance level"] C -->|No| E["Stop and investigate"] Mermaid source mermaid flowchart TD A["Validate authentication transaction and callback"] --> B["Resolve verified identity to active membership"] B --> C{"Acceptance and policy pass"} C -->|Yes| D["Create a session at the required assurance level"] C -->|No| E["Stop and investigate"] 8. Failure Modes, Edge Cases and Security Failure Containment Account linking trusts unverified email Stop the affected operation; inspect its last durable boundary and redacted evidence. Reconcile uncertain side effects before retrying and add a regression case. Recovery bypasses the primary factor Stop the affected operation; inspect its last durable boundary and redacted evidence. Reconcile uncertain side effects before retrying and add a regression case. Authorize tenant-owned inputs and artifacts explicitly. Distinguish permanent validation failures from transient dependency errors. Exclude raw session tokens, credentials, OTPs and private content from routine logs. 9. Acceptance, Testing and Verification Matrix Case Expected outcome Evidence Tampered callback is rejected Condition holds in the intended environment; failure blocks approval. Tested revision, input, observed result and reviewer Suspended identity cannot create sessions Condition holds in the intended environment; failure blocks approval. Tested revision, input, observed result and reviewer Priority negative paths Account linking trusts unverified email; Recovery bypasses the primary factor Reproduction and containment Standalone HTML Complete chapter is readable before JavaScript executes Inspect source and disable JavaScript Copy and Mermaid Exact source remains available without diagram preview Copy/paste and module-load failure checks 10. Operations, Ownership and Maintenance Assign a technical owner for authentication & sso. Review changes to Duo, WebAuthn, OIDC provider against this chapter’s assumptions. Record the dependency contract, environment and last tested revision. Use the failure matrix to locate uncertain state during incidents. Preserve redacted evidence, restore the approved configuration or apply a reviewed correction, and rerun acceptance checks. Update the review date after provider or architectural changes. 11. Official References and Source Scope These authoritative references are mapped specifically to this chapter. The daily checker compares source titles and a bounded heading outline; it does not certify every technical claim or rewrite examples automatically. https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html https://openid.net/specs/openid-connect-core-1_0.html 12. Prerequisites, Related Chapters and Next Steps Learning path: Application Platform Start with the first chapter below when you need background, then use the remaining chapters to connect this topic to implementation and verification. Suggested prerequisite Sessions & Authorization Enforce operation permissions and revocation after identity verification. Related implementation Email OTP & Recovery Implement challenge issuance, expiry, resend and atomic verification. Related implementation Email Delivery Deliver security and transactional messages through authenticated SMTP. Completion evidence: record how this chapter’s process connects to its upstream identity or data input, its downstream operation, and the tests that verify the boundary. If a related dependency changes, review both chapters together. 13. Daily Reference Updates Daily checking is scheduled for this chapter at 08:10 Malaysia time. Source-check results load when the update service is available. Source checks and editorial review are different. A source outline change is a review signal, not proof of a changed API contract. chapters.text: CHAPTER 22 · ENGINEERING KNOWLEDGE Production AI Application Architecture Version Reviewed Architecture scope 2.0.0 2 November 2026 Route compatible requests to approved models within budget and policy. On this page 1. Description, Purpose and Boundaries 2. Architectural Principles and Decisions 3. Process, Inputs and Outputs 4. Related Apps, Software and Third Parties 5. Detailed Architecture, Implementation and Tests 6. Implementation Pattern and Copyable Code 7. Mermaid Architecture and Process Diagram 8. Failure Modes, Edge Cases and Security 9. Acceptance, Testing and Verification Matrix 10. Operations, Ownership and Maintenance 11. Official References and Source Scope 12. Prerequisites, Related Chapters and Next Steps 13. Daily Reference Updates 1. Description, Purpose and Boundaries Route compatible requests to approved models within budget and policy. Route by required capability and validated performance, then optimize cost. Treat model outputs and proposed tool calls as untrusted. Treat model routing & evaluation as an independently reviewable capability. Trace its inputs, processing decisions and acceptance evidence before applying it to a live system. The examples define bounded units; external services need separately verified permissions, contracts and environment configuration. 2. Architectural Principles and Decisions The primary decision boundary is: Reserve budget and invoke approved adapter. Application logic and an accountable owner establish this decision. Preserve the input identity and rule revision so its outcome can be investigated. Prioritize fallback weakens data policy and timeout releases budget despite uncertain charge. Establish checks for these failures before enabling automation. Completion requires evidence for the final step, validate output and settle or reconcile usage, rather than merely observing request acceptance. 3. Process, Inputs and Outputs Step Action Evidence 1 Validate task contract and capability requirements Approved input scope, source and owner 2 Reserve budget and invoke approved adapter Recorded decision, revision and exception handling 3 Validate output and settle or reconcile usage Observed outcome and recovery or rollback decision Stop at any boundary whose required evidence cannot be established. If an external side effect may already have occurred, reconcile its durable identity before retrying. 4. Related Apps, Software and Third Parties Component Role Integration responsibility Model registry Approved provider contracts Verify supported contract, least privilege, account access, data handling, quotas and ownership. Budget ledger Admission accounting Verify supported contract, least privilege, account access, data handling, quotas and ownership. Model adapter Transport boundary Verify supported contract, least privilege, account access, data handling, quotas and ownership. These products are candidates for this capability, not a claim that they are connected to this documentation site. Choose them by boundary responsibility and measured requirements. Keep their private credentials outside public HTML. 5. Detailed Architecture, Implementation and Tests Page 1 — Production AI Application Architecture and Request Lifecycle Metadata Value Document version 1.0.0 Last reviewed 2 November 2026 Target scope Tenant-aware, server-controlled AI inference service; TypeScript application core; GitHub CI; Cloudflare application hosting; managed model adapters Audience Platform engineers, application developers, security reviewers and operations owners Implementation boundary A complete, provider-independent request-lifecycle module and executable acceptance tests. Identity verification, durable accounting and provider transport are explicit service contracts. Release status Architecture reference. Production approval requires the verification matrix below to pass against the actual deployed dependencies. 1. Architectural overview and governing principles An AI application must control more than model invocation. It must determine who is asking, which tenant owns the request, whether the requested operation is permitted, which data may leave the system, how much work is affordable, and what happens if the client or provider fails halfway through processing. The model is an untrusted computational dependency. It does not establish identity, assign roles, choose unrestricted network destinations or authorize side effects. The application makes these decisions before invoking it and validates its result afterward. A model-generated string cannot change a permission policy. The request lifecycle below supports bounded text inference without tools. Tool execution, retrieval, email delivery and account enrollment are separate service capabilities. Their absence is deliberate: an inference endpoint must not accidentally acquire authority to send messages or mutate business records simply because a model supports function calling. 1.1 Trust boundaries flowchart TD U["Untrusted client"] --> G["Request gateway"] G --> I["Identity and tenant checks"] I --> A{"Admission policy"} A -->|Reject| R["Safe error"] A -->|Admit| B["Durable budget reservation"] B --> M["Scoped model adapter"] M --> V["Response validation"] V --> S["Accounting settlement"] S --> O["Response and redacted audit"] Mermaid source flowchart TD U["Untrusted client"] --> G["Request gateway"] G --> I["Identity and tenant checks"] I --> A{"Admission policy"} A -->|Reject| R["Safe error"] A -->|Admit| B["Durable budget reservation"] B --> M["Scoped model adapter"] M --> V["Response validation"] V --> S["Accounting settlement"] S --> O["Response and redacted audit"] The client boundary accepts only a task name, an input string and an output-token ceiling. Tenant membership and permissions arrive from authenticated server state. The adapter boundary translates the application contract into one provider's current API. Budget enforcement happens in a durable accounting boundary shared by all application instances. Each boundary has an independent failure policy. Authentication failure must not fall through to an anonymous paid request. Budget failure must not invoke the model. A provider timeout is an uncertain outcome because processing may continue remotely. A settlement failure must not silently discard the accounting obligation. 1.2 Non-negotiable invariants 1. Every admitted request has a verified principal with an active tenant membership. 2. Every model call follows a successful budget reservation. 3. The reservation precedes the side effect and includes a unique request identifier. 4. Provider selection comes from an approved server registry, never a client-supplied URL. 5. Unsupported tasks and token limits fail before provider invocation. 6. A timeout or transport failure retains its reservation until reconciliation establishes usage or releases it safely. 7. Prompts, API credentials, session tokens and generated private text are excluded from routine logs. 8. The provider's answer remains data. Rendering it must not execute HTML, scripts or commands. 2. Detailed system mechanics 2.1 Identity and authorization The HTTP authentication layer verifies the session or access token and constructs a Principal. The principal's user ID, tenant ID and permission set must come from the verified identity and membership records. A browser-submitted tenant header is merely a requested tenant and must be checked against membership. A permission check applies to the operation, not just the page. A user who can view the chat interface does not automatically have permission to invoke every model, export tenant knowledge or execute administrative tools. The reference module requires the ai:generate permission and an active membership. Permission changes introduce cache invalidation requirements. A suspended account must lose access within the defined revocation window. If membership is cached, document the maximum stale interval and bypass that cache for privileged actions. Tokens with tenant or role claims require server-side validation and a strategy for revocation. 2.2 Input boundaries and token accounting Limit HTTP body bytes before parsing JSON. After parsing, reject unknown properties, invalid types, blank inputs and unsupported tasks. A character limit is not a token estimate: UTF-8 byte length, Unicode code points and provider tokenization differ. The accounting service must reserve a conservative upper bound derived from the full provider request: developer instructions, user input, retrieved context, tool schemas, image/audio charges when applicable, the output ceiling and the provider's billing model. The reference uses reservation units rather than money to avoid pretending that a single universal price calculation fits every model. Provider usage is authoritative only after validating the response schema. Missing usage is an accounting uncertainty, not zero cost. For metered production systems, reconcile provider billing records against application reservations. 2.3 Registry and task routing A registry entry records the task, adapter key, approved model ID, token ceiling and data-processing policy. At deployment, validate each entry against the provider's current capability schema. A model supporting text input does not necessarily support a particular structured-output format, tool schema or reasoning parameter. As of this review, official catalogs list GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6.1 Terra and GPT-6 Luna; Claude Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5; and Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 3.8 Flash. These are candidate families, not interchangeable endpoint contracts. Choose a model using representative task evaluations and verify account availability. The code below intentionally does not hardcode a provider or a model alias. 2.4 Budget lifecycle and uncertain completion stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Reserved: atomic admission Reserved --> Settled: verified usage Reserved --> HeldForReconciliation: timeout or unknown outcome HeldForReconciliation --> Settled: usage recovered HeldForReconciliation --> Released: confirmed no charge Settled --> [*] Released --> [*] Mermaid source stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Reserved: atomic admission Reserved --> Settled: verified usage Reserved --> HeldForReconciliation: timeout or unknown outcome HeldForReconciliation --> Settled: usage recovered HeldForReconciliation --> Released: confirmed no charge Settled --> [*] Released --> [*] A reservation is not an in-memory counter. Implement it with a transactional store or a coordination mechanism that can atomically compare the tenant's available allowance and create the reservation. Concurrent requests must not overspend by observing the same balance. Reservation IDs and request IDs must be unique within the intended scope. A retry of an already completed request should retrieve the persisted result or return its existing status instead of spending again. This module generates a new request ID per execution and does not claim HTTP-level idempotency. Add a durable idempotency coordinator before exposing retryable paid mutations. The adapter may fail after a provider accepted the request. Releasing the entire reservation on every exception allows repeated uncertain requests to bypass spending limits. The safe default is to retain the reservation and enqueue reconciliation. Record expiry and escalation rules so held funds do not remain locked forever. 2.5 Timeouts, cancellation and retries Propagate AbortSignal to the provider transport. A local abort does not prove that the remote provider stopped computation. The deadline implementation races the transport promise so the caller is bounded even if an adapter fails to honor cancellation. Do not retry a model call automatically after an ambiguous timeout. Retrying can duplicate charges and produce two divergent outputs. Explicit retries must pass admission again and honor the request's durable idempotency state. Rate-limit responses may support a delayed retry, but only within a documented attempt and time budget. 2.6 Output safety An adapter returns text and measured usage through a narrow object contract. The core rejects empty answers, oversized UTF-8 responses and malformed usage. A provider's refusal, incomplete generation and tool-call response require explicit adapter handling; they must not be disguised as successful plain-text completion. Render model output as text or sanitized Markdown. Do not place it in an unsanitized innerHTML assignment. Treat generated URLs, shell commands, SQL statements and email recipients as untrusted proposals requiring separate validation and authorization. 3. Production implementation pattern The following TypeScript module has no third-party runtime dependencies. It can be compiled with TypeScript targeting ES2022 and the DOM library. It defines all application contracts and the complete orchestration logic within this chapter's boundary. 3.1 src/lifecycle.ts export type Task = "assistant" | "code_review"; export interface Principal { userId: string; tenantId: string; membershipActive: boolean; permissions: ReadonlySet<string>; } export interface GenerationRequest { task: Task; input: string; maxOutputTokens: number; } export interface ModelPolicy { adapterKey: string; modelId: string; maxOutputTokens: number; } export interface Usage { inputTokens: number; outputTokens: number; } export interface ModelResult { text: string; usage: Usage; } export interface ModelAdapter { generate( policy: ModelPolicy, request: GenerationRequest, signal: AbortSignal ): Promise<ModelResult>; } export interface BudgetLedger { reserve(input: { requestId: string; tenantId: string; policy: ModelPolicy; request: GenerationRequest; }): Promise<{ reservationId: string }>; settle(reservationId: string, usage: Usage): Promise<void>; holdForReconciliation( reservationId: string, requestId: string ): Promise<void>; } export interface AuditEvent { requestId: string; tenantId: string; task: Task; outcome: "completed" | "failed" | "reconciliation_failed"; durationMs: number; } export interface Dependencies { policies: Readonly<Record<Task, ModelPolicy>>; adapters: ReadonlyMap<string, ModelAdapter>; ledger: BudgetLedger; audit(event: AuditEvent): void; now(): number; requestId(): string; timeoutMs: number; maxAnswerBytes: number; } export class LifecycleError extends Error { constructor( public readonly code: string, public readonly httpStatus: number ) { super(code); this.name = "LifecycleError"; } } export function parseRequest(value: unknown): GenerationRequest { if (!value || typeof value !== "object" || Array.isArray(value)) { throw new LifecycleError("invalid_request", 400); } const item = value as Record<string, unknown>; const allowed = new Set(["task", "input", "maxOutputTokens"]); if (Object.keys(item).some((key) => !allowed.has(key))) { throw new LifecycleError("unknown_property", 400); } if (item.task !== "assistant" && item.task !== "code_review") { throw new LifecycleError("unsupported_task", 400); } if ( typeof item.input !== "string" || item.input.trim().length === 0 || new TextEncoder().encode(item.input).byteLength > 16_384 ) { throw new LifecycleError("invalid_input", 400); } if ( typeof item.maxOutputTokens !== "number" || !Number.isSafeInteger(item.maxOutputTokens) || item.maxOutputTokens < 1 || item.maxOutputTokens > 4_096 ) { throw new LifecycleError("invalid_output_limit", 400); } return { task: item.task, input: item.input, maxOutputTokens: item.maxOutputTokens }; } function validateUsage(usage: Usage): void { if ( !usage || !Number.isSafeInteger(usage.inputTokens) || usage.inputTokens < 0 || !Number.isSafeInteger(usage.outputTokens) || usage.outputTokens < 0 ) { throw new LifecycleError("invalid_provider_usage", 502); } } export async function generate( principal: Principal, raw: unknown, deps: Dependencies ): Promise<{ requestId: string; text: string; usage: Usage }> { if ( !principal.userId || !principal.tenantId || !principal.membershipActive || !principal.permissions.has("ai:generate") ) { throw new LifecycleError("forbidden", 403); } const request = parseRequest(raw); const policy = deps.policies[request.task]; if ( !policy || !policy.modelId || request.maxOutputTokens > policy.maxOutputTokens ) { throw new LifecycleError("task_policy_rejected", 400); } const adapter = deps.adapters.get(policy.adapterKey); if (!adapter) { throw new LifecycleError("adapter_unavailable", 503); } if ( !Number.isSafeInteger(deps.timeoutMs) || deps.timeoutMs < 1 || !Number.isSafeInteger(deps.maxAnswerBytes) || deps.maxAnswerBytes < 1 ) { throw new LifecycleError("invalid_runtime_policy", 503); } const requestId = deps.requestId(); const started = deps.now(); const reservation = await deps.ledger.reserve({ requestId, tenantId: principal.tenantId, policy, request }); let timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined; const controller = new AbortController(); const emit = (outcome: AuditEvent["outcome"]): void => { try { deps.audit({ requestId, tenantId: principal.tenantId, task: request.task, outcome, durationMs: Math.max(0, deps.now() - started) }); } catch { // Audit transport health must be monitored independently. // Never expose private provider errors through this path. } }; try { const deadline = new Promise<never>((_, reject) => { timer = setTimeout(() => { controller.abort(); reject(new LifecycleError("provider_timeout", 504)); }, deps.timeoutMs); }); const result = await Promise.race([ adapter.generate(policy, request, controller.signal), deadline ]); validateUsage(result.usage); if ( typeof result.text !== "string" || result.text.trim().length === 0 || new TextEncoder().encode(result.text).byteLength > deps.maxAnswerBytes ) { throw new LifecycleError("invalid_provider_output", 502); } await deps.ledger.settle(reservation.reservationId, result.usage); emit("completed"); return { requestId, text: result.text, usage: result.usage }; } catch (error) { try { await deps.ledger.holdForReconciliation( reservation.reservationId, requestId ); } catch { emit("reconciliation_failed"); } emit("failed"); if (error instanceof LifecycleError) { throw error; } throw new LifecycleError("generation_failed", 502); } finally { if (timer !== undefined) { clearTimeout(timer); } } } 3.2 Contract requirements for dependency implementations The ledger's reserve operation must reject exhausted or suspended tenants before returning a reservation ID. Settle must be idempotent and must not double-charge when the same usage is submitted twice. Hold must not overwrite a previously settled reservation. Because settlement itself can fail after committing, reconciliation must inspect durable state before applying another charge. Ledger operations require their own bounded storage deadlines. The model deadline does not bound a stalled database call. The HTTP host should enforce an overall request deadline and reserve time for reconciliation or dispatch that work durably. An execution context's background callback is not a substitute for a durable queue when losing work would lose billing records. The adapter must enforce its own response-body size limit before parsing, translate provider-specific refusal/incomplete states into typed failures, and validate usage fields. It must not accept a request-provided base URL. API credentials belong in managed secrets and must not appear in policies or audit events. The audit implementation should be nonblocking and feed a monitored transport with a defined loss policy. A deployment requiring fail-closed compliance audit must reject admission when durable audit is unavailable; the reference's best-effort telemetry hook does not satisfy that stronger requirement. 4. Complete executable acceptance test The test uses an in-memory ledger only as a deterministic test double. It is not a production accounting implementation and does not claim distributed atomicity. 4.1 src/lifecycle.test.ts import { generate, LifecycleError, type BudgetLedger, type Dependencies, type ModelAdapter, type Principal, type Usage } from "./lifecycle.js"; function assert(condition: unknown, message: string): asserts condition { if (!condition) throw new Error(message); } async function rejects( operation: () => Promise<unknown>, code: string ): Promise<void> { try { await operation(); } catch (error) { assert(error instanceof LifecycleError, "Expected LifecycleError"); assert(error.code === code, "Unexpected error code"); return; } throw new Error("Expected rejection"); } const states = new Map<string, string>(); let reservations = 0; let adapterCalls = 0; const ledger: BudgetLedger = { async reserve(input) { reservations += 1; states.set(input.requestId, "reserved"); return { reservationId: input.requestId }; }, async settle(id: string, usage: Usage) { assert(usage.outputTokens >= 0, "Invalid usage"); states.set(id, "settled"); }, async holdForReconciliation(id: string) { if (states.get(id) !== "settled") states.set(id, "held"); } }; const adapter: ModelAdapter = { async generate() { adapterCalls += 1; return { text: "Validated response", usage: { inputTokens: 12, outputTokens: 4 } }; } }; let sequence = 0; const deps: Dependencies = { policies: { assistant: { adapterKey: "test", modelId: "deterministic-test-adapter", maxOutputTokens: 1024 }, code_review: { adapterKey: "test", modelId: "deterministic-test-adapter", maxOutputTokens: 1024 } }, adapters: new Map([["test", adapter]]), ledger, audit() {}, now: () => Date.now(), requestId: () => "request-" + (++sequence), timeoutMs: 50, maxAnswerBytes: 4096 }; const principal: Principal = { userId: "test-user", tenantId: "test-tenant", membershipActive: true, permissions: new Set(["ai:generate"]) }; const input = { task: "assistant", input: "Explain a transactional outbox.", maxOutputTokens: 128 }; const result = await generate(principal, input, deps); assert(result.text === "Validated response", "Wrong response"); assert(states.get(result.requestId) === "settled", "Not settled"); const beforeDenied = reservations; await rejects( () => generate({ ...principal, membershipActive: false }, input, deps), "forbidden" ); assert(reservations === beforeDenied, "Denied request reserved budget"); await rejects( () => generate(principal, { ...input, model: "client-choice" }, deps), "unknown_property" ); const failing: ModelAdapter = { async generate() { throw new Error("Sensitive upstream detail"); } }; await rejects( () => generate(principal, input, { ...deps, adapters: new Map([["test", failing]]) }), "generation_failed" ); assert(states.get("request-" + sequence) === "held", "Failure not held"); const stalled: ModelAdapter = { async generate() { return new Promise(() => {}); } }; await rejects( () => generate(principal, input, { ...deps, timeoutMs: 5, adapters: new Map([["test", stalled]]) }), "provider_timeout" ); assert(states.get("request-" + sequence) === "held", "Timeout not held"); assert(adapterCalls === 1, "Unexpected successful adapter calls"); console.log("Lifecycle acceptance tests passed"); 4.2 Compiler configuration Save this complete configuration as tsconfig.json. Install TypeScript as a development dependency, commit the generated package lock, and use the same locked compiler in CI. { "compilerOptions": { "target": "ES2022", "module": "NodeNext", "moduleResolution": "NodeNext", "lib": ["ES2022", "DOM"], "strict": true, "outDir": "dist", "rootDir": "src", "skipLibCheck": true, "noEmitOnError": true }, "include": ["src/**/*.ts"] } Set the package's type field to module so the test's top-level await uses ECMAScript modules. Run the compiler followed by the emitted test: npm pkg set type=module npm install --save-dev typescript npx tsc --project tsconfig.json node dist/lifecycle.test.js Do not substitute synthetic model IDs into a live provider. The deterministic-test-adapter string is a real test fixture identifier consumed only by the test double. 5. Deployment configuration and secret boundaries This chapter's module does not start a public HTTP listener. Integrate it behind the application's authenticated gateway, then bind concrete ledger and provider adapters. Publishing a raw unauthenticated wrapper would violate the invariants in Section 1. For a Cloudflare deployment, keep the compatibility date explicit and use version-controlled non-secret configuration. Provision provider credentials as Worker secrets or approved Secret Store bindings. Verify each environment separately because resource and secret binding behavior must not be assumed to inherit across environments. The following is an application policy document, not a Wrangler manifest. An admission configuration loader must validate every property and reject unknown keys. version: 1 request_policy: maximum_body_bytes: 24576 maximum_input_utf8_bytes: 16384 maximum_output_tokens: 4096 maximum_answer_utf8_bytes: 65536 model_deadline_ms: 25000 require_active_membership: true required_permission: ai:generate automatic_provider_retries: 0 accounting_policy: reserve_before_inference: true unknown_outcome: hold_for_reconciliation settlement_idempotency: required logging_policy: include_request_id: true include_tenant_id: true include_duration: true include_prompt: false include_generated_text: false include_credentials: false The limits are deliberately local policy values, not provider quotas. The gateway body limit is larger than the input-string limit to allow JSON syntax and metadata while bounding memory use. The output byte ceiling is independent of output-token limits. A generated Unicode answer can consume more bytes than its visible length suggests. A Docker image is not needed for the Workers runtime. Container deployment is a separate target requiring its own HTTP server, signal handling, health checks and secret injection. Including a nonfunctional Dockerfile would make this chapter less complete, not more deployable. 6. Acceptance, testing and verification matrix Area Concrete test Required result Identity Expired session reaches gateway 401 before lifecycle invocation; no reservation or model call Authorization Inactive membership or missing permission 403; no provider activity Tenant isolation Client changes tenant header or object ID Membership check rejects unauthorized tenant Input schema Unknown property, blank input, array body, unsupported task 400 before reservation Unicode Input exceeds 16,384 UTF-8 bytes with multibyte characters Rejected using encoded byte length Token policy Output ceiling exceeds registry maximum Rejected before inference Registry Adapter missing or model unapproved Fail closed; no user-controlled fallback Budget concurrency Parallel requests compete for final allowance Durable ledger admits only affordable reservations Successful completion Adapter returns valid text and usage Exactly one idempotent settlement and safe response Provider transport Connection resets after request submission Reservation retained for reconciliation Timeout Adapter ignores AbortSignal Caller still receives bounded timeout Output Empty text, oversized bytes or invalid usage 502; uncertain spend remains reserved Settlement uncertainty Database commits then connection fails Reconciliation reads existing state; no duplicate charge Telemetry Audit destination fails Alert under defined loss policy; no credential leakage Rendering Model emits script, HTML or executable command Displayed as inert data; no automatic execution Retry Client resubmits a paid request Durable idempotency coordinator applies documented replay policy Recovery Held reservation exceeds reconciliation objective Alert and audited investigation; no silent release Secrets Inspect static assets and logs No provider keys, OTPs, bearer tokens or private prompts Rollback Registry version regresses quality Restore approved version without weakening authorization 6.1 Operational objectives Define service objectives before launch: admission availability, successful-request latency, timeout rate, unresolved-reservation age and cost per accepted task. Set thresholds from measured staging traffic and the business risk profile. The chapter does not invent universal production percentages. Alert on oldest unresolved reservation, repeated settlement errors, provider authorization failures and unexpected token growth. A model outage should degrade the AI feature while preserving identity, accounting records and ordinary application access. 6.2 Known implementation traps An in-memory limiter is instance-local and cannot enforce a global tenant allowance. A provider API key scoped to a whole organization can exceed the authority needed by one application. A fallback model with different retention terms can violate a data-processing policy even when its output is correct. Filter incompatible models before ranking candidates. Use the least expensive candidate that meets the measured quality bar; escalate only when policy and budget permit. Registry and fallbacks Store provider, exact model ID, version or snapshot, verified capabilities, region, quotas, evaluation version, approved_at and rollback target. Distinguish transient capacity errors from unsupported requests and policy refusals. Do not use a fallback that weakens privacy, tool permissions or output schema. Use paired task comparisons and enough representative examples; report uncertainty. A self-rating by the generating model is not a substitute for an independent acceptance test. RAG, tuning and long context Use retrieval for changing or private knowledge with access filtering and provenance. Use fine-tuning only when measured behavior/style improvements justify dataset and maintenance costs. Use long context when the task needs it and test lost-in-context failures. Track drift on production-like samples. Model changes must not alter account authorization or allow retrieved instructions to override policy. 6. Return an opaque challenge identifier and a generic acknowledgement. Bind the stored challenge to identity, purpose and expiry. For short numeric codes, store a keyed HMAC verifier with a separately protected server key; an ordinary hash alone is easy to enumerate offline. Never log or return the code. Example policy and data Example: an eight-digit code, five-minute lifetime, five verification attempts and a 60-second resend cooldown. Tune limits to risk and usability and apply aggregate limits by account and network. Store id, user or normalized identity reference, purpose, verifier, expires_at, attempts, consumed_at and generation. Make resend behavior explicit: invalidate the previous generation and clearly tell users only the newest code works. Atomic verification POST /auth/otp/verify checks expiry, purpose, generation and attempt budget server-side. Avoid relying on email-link GET requests to consume credentials because mail scanners may prefetch links. The Worker independently retrieves public references, records a bounded source outline and exposes its results through read-only JSON endpoints. The service does not execute a language model, rewrite chapter prose, modify code, send email or commit to GitHub. A detected title or heading change signals that an editor should review the affected narrative. This distinction prevents an automated availability check from being presented as verified technical advice. 2. Architectural Principles and Decisions The static site and updater have separate release and failure boundaries. A source outage or unavailable Worker must not prevent reading the complete chapter. Browser requests contain only the public chapter identifier. No credentials or private chapter content are sent to the updater. The registry fixes chapter IDs and reference URLs at deployment. Readers cannot supply arbitrary URLs, trigger refreshes or mutate state. Fetches require HTTPS, reject unapproved destination hosts, follow at most two approved redirects and apply an eight-second timeout plus a 256 KiB document-prefix limit. The comparison covers the title and first five main-content headings when available; it is not a complete semantic or code diff. 3.
